commentary.bottom_line: No supplied study tests whether standardized pre-deployment procedures for patient disclosure or consent change how consistently patients are informed, and no supplied study documents the size of the inconsistency. The recommendation rests on three framework and guidance endorsements, one of which addresses oversight roles in general rather than disclosure.

perspectives.view: Zero studies test the practice and zero studies document the hazard, so certainty cannot be rated above no direct evidence. The three endorsements are expert frameworks and guidance, which GRADE treats as opinion rather than evidence. The CHAI playbook statement concerns assigning oversight responsibility, which bears on disclosure only indirectly.

The endorsements come from voluntary frameworks and professional guidance, not from statute or regulation. One uses must language about naming responsible parties, and two use should language about transparency and ethical norms for disclosure. None of the supplied sources specifies what disclosure content, timing, or consent threshold a standardized procedure should apply.

commentary.research_gap: Studies are needed that compare health systems or deployments with and without a standardized disclosure and consent procedure, measuring how consistently patients are informed, patient understanding and trust, staff time required, and whether decisions differ by type of AI tool. Descriptive studies measuring current variation in disclosure practice would establish whether the hazard exists at meaningful scale.
commentary.underserved_note: No study tested the practice, so no test included Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. It is unknown whether standardized procedures would produce disclosures that these patients can understand, or whether consent processes would place added burden on them.
